title: From learning analytics to educational interventions: enhancing decision-making and learning design
abstract: Abstract Since the early development of learning analytics (LA), the cyclical nature of the process that starts with learning data and ends with educational interventions has been widely acknowledged. However, while LA research abounds, and LA practices are becoming more widespread, the final step of the cycle – introducing educational interventions - remains a challenge. The recently revised definition of LA puts a stronger focus on actionable insights to enhance learning and teaching. Recognizing that only trustworthy LA presents a basis for meaningful educational interventions, we conducted a study relying on group decision-making to explore and determine the key enablers of LA-based educational interventions. Our findings revealed seven enablers: institutional strategic orientation , pedagogical & other research foundations , available resources , pedagogical support , ethics & data governance , stakeholder engagement , and quality assurance . These enablers provide a foundation for the development and use of trustworthy LA systems to support data-informed decision-making, learning design, and educational change.

title: Knowing its name, not its nature: word association mapping of student AI cognition and evidence-based micro-credential design in Turkish higher education
abstract: Abstract Although artificial intelligence (AI) tools are now deeply embedded in Turkish university students’ academic lives, students’ cognitive representations of AI remain instrumentally oriented and structurally fragmented. This study presents a needs assessment for designing AI literacy micro-credential programmes grounded in learners’ actual knowledge structures. Using the Word Association Test (WAT) as a psycholinguistic cognitive diagnostic instrument, data were collected from N = 436 undergraduate students enrolled at four public universities in Turkey (Kırklareli, İnönü, Niğde Ömer Halisdemir, and Hatay Mustafa Kemal), representing social sciences and humanities (80.3%), natural and applied sciences (12.2%), and health sciences (7.6%). WAT responses (1376 raw tokens) were analysed through a seven-stage protocol comprising canonical code taxonomy (65 codes; inter-rater reliability κ = 0.87), Kendall’s τ relatedness estimation with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, multidimensional scaling (stress = 0.396), hierarchical threshold network construction, and Z-score band analysis. Findings reveal a consistent pattern of cognitive fragmentation: utilitarian concepts-most prominently convenience (f = 145), speed, and technology-dominate students’ associative networks, while algorithmic transparency, ethical governance, and technical mechanisms remain conceptually absent. Network analysis reveals structural polarisation between positive-utility and negative-risk clusters (τ = − 0.819), confirming a pervasive ‘black-box’ orientation toward AI. Utilising these diagnostic findings as a curriculum roadmap, the study proposes an Ethical AI and Workforce Readiness micro-credential framework that bridges the gap between functional use and conceptual mastery. This study contributes the first large-scale WAT-based cognitive mapping of AI knowledge structures in Turkish higher education and demonstrates a replicable, data-driven methodology for needs-assessment-driven credential design.
journal_title: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education

title: From insight to intervention: learning analytics and generative AI support for learning design and educational decision-making
abstract: Abstract Recent advances in learning design tools, learning analytics, and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have created new possibilities for educators to design, monitor, and adapt learning experiences. Yet evidence that these possibilities routinely translate into student-centred, inclusive, personalised, and effective practice remains limited. This editorial synthesises four contributions to the special issue on learning analytics and AI support for learning design and educational decision-making. Across student, teacher, disciplinary, and institutional levels, the studies show that technology does not become educationally valuable through technical capability alone. Its value is mediated by learning design, community and interaction, digital literacy, educator and learner agency, ethical fitness, organisational strategy, resources, and wide stakeholder engagement. At the same time, the evidence base remains dominated by cross-sectional, self-report, discourse-based, and expert-judgement studies. We argue that the field must now move from demonstrating associations and proposing frameworks towards intervention research that tests causal mechanisms, implementation conditions, longer-term outcomes, and distributional effects. A future agenda should connect learning analytics and GenAI tightly to educational visions, pedagogical intentions, preserve human and epistemic agency, and build trustworthy socio-technical infrastructures that enable educators and learners to act on evidence.
journal_title: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education

title: Guarded adoption of generative AI in higher education: high-achieving students, successful-student identity, and epistemic agency in a single-university mixed-methods survey
abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence is becoming part of university learning, but students do not engage with it uniformly. This mixed-methods survey of students at one Australian university examined whether successful-student identity and student-reported academic achievement were associated with different patterns of generative AI engagement. The institution-wide survey yielded 484 responses, including 469 with valid GPA-band data. Higher-achieving students reported lower active AI engagement, positive affect, perceived learning impact, and AI-related disengagement, alongside slightly higher negative affect. Item-level analyses showed less endorsement of AI-supported autonomy, effective learning, and active engagement, and greater agreement that reliance on AI hinders critical thinking and independent problem solving. Open-ended responses indicated that these students used AI selectively for clarification, summarisation, and workflow support while checking outputs and keeping them subordinate to their own judgment. The paper interprets this pattern as guarded adoption: selective, bounded, and verification-intensive use in defence of epistemic control and successful-student identity.

title: AI-Supported lecturer decision-making in higher education: a socio-technical perspective
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) has become an integral part of teaching and learning in higher education. Through its capacity to generate actionable insights from student data, AI systems provide new opportunities to support lecturers’ decision-making. However, it remains unclear how AI systems support and mediate lecturer decision-making across different decision types. Existing research has primarily focused on technical capabilities and learning outcomes, while paying limited attention to the socio-technical dynamics of AI-supported lecturer decision-making. To address this gap, this study develops an empirically grounded taxonomy of AI-supported lecturer decision-making and maps the relationships among decision types, AI systems, student data, and learning outcomes. Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic literature review of 27 empirical studies published between 2016 and 2025 was conducted using qualitative content analysis. The findings identify eight lecturer decision types and show that AI support is concentrated in instructional, feedback, and assessment decisions, while emotional, ethical, administrative, curriculum, and learning-environment decisions remain underrepresented. Learning Analytics Dashboards were the most frequently reported system type, primarily supporting monitoring, feedback, and assessment functions based on textual and log data. From a socio-technical perspective, the AI systems described in this sample predominantly made behavioral student data visible and actionable for lecturers, and the decisions they supported were correspondingly concentrated in instructional, assessment, and feedback domains, while processes related to motivation, metacognition, emotions, and learning environments received far less support. These findings highlight an important gap: How can alternative forms of student data visibility, attentional guidance, and interface design support lecturer decisions?

title: Large language models for teaching and learning in higher education: opportunities, challenges, and future directions
abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly reshaping the technological landscape of higher education, extending from conversational assistance and personalized learning to assessment, recommendation, and institutional services. Yet their educational value cannot be inferred from generative capability alone. What matters is how these models are incorporated into educational practice and institutional systems, and what forms of human oversight accompany their use. This editorial introduces the special issue “Harnessing Large Language Models for Teaching and Learning: Challenges, Opportunities, and Future Directions,” comprising five contributions that examine LLM-enhanced course recommendation, real-time prompting support, automated essay scoring, verifiable online education, and knowledge-augmented automation for higher-education services. Taken together, these contributions illustrate how LLMs are increasingly being used as components of educational systems rather than as stand-alone generative tools. Across the collection, the potential benefits are clearest where LLM capabilities are tied to specific educational or institutional needs. At the same time, the collection exposes a persistent gap between technical performance and evidence of educational effectiveness. Many of the questions that matter most for practice, particularly those concerning learner development, use in authentic settings, and institutional responsibility, remain insufficiently examined. We argue that future research should move beyond demonstrating what LLMs can accomplish toward establishing when, for whom, and under what pedagogical and institutional conditions their use produces meaningful educational value. This shift calls for research grounded in educational theory and tested in authentic settings, with explicit attention to how responsibility is distributed between people and AI systems. The technically diverse contributions in this special issue provide a foundation for this broader research agenda.

title: Seeing what students learn: assessing cognitive representations and academic outcomes via EEG image reconstruction
abstract: Abstract Understanding how humans process visual information during learning remains a central challenge in cognitive neuroscience. Traditional approaches typically rely on behavioral observations or indirect neural measures, which limits direct insight into learners’ internal cognitive representations. Recent advances in brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) and deep learning have enabled image reconstruction from electroencephalography (EEG), providing a promising pathway to decode latent cognitive states. In this study, we investigate how EEG-based image reconstruction relates to students’ learning. While students watched educational videos, we recorded EEG signals and used an image reconstruction model to generate images reflecting their perceived visual representations. We assessed reconstruction quality using semantic similarity between reconstructed and original images. First, we examine whether semantic similarity is associated with overall academic performance and find a significant positive association in our sample. Second, we evaluate item-level effects and show that questions answered incorrectly correspond to significantly lower semantic similarity than correctly answered questions. Third, we analyze the temporal dynamics of reconstruction and demonstrate that temporal misalignment patterns—quantified through dispersion-related measures—are associated with learners’ performance. Overall, these exploratory results provide preliminary evidence that EEG-based image reconstruction is sensitive to both the strength and the temporal evolution of learners’ cognitive representations. If replicated in larger and more diverse samples, this approach may offer a promising direction for studying learning processes and for informing more personalized, data-driven educational interventions.

title: Human–AI collaborative patterns in GenAI-supported instructional design among pre-service teachers: an analysis of interaction sequences and cognitive load
abstract: Abstract The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence is profoundly reshaping the paradigm of instructional design. However, the micro-level process patterns of human-AI collaboration in generative AI-enabled instructional design for pre-service teachers still require in-depth analysis. This study aims to uncover the behavioral patterns and cognitive load characteristics of pre-service teachers when collaborating with generative AI to complete instructional design tasks and to explore the patterns of efficient human-AI collaboration. A total of 67 pre-service teachers completed instructional design tasks with AI assistance. A systematic instructional plan quality evaluation rubric was developed based on relevant theories, and participants were assigned to the high-quality and low-quality groups using a median split of their lesson-plan quality scores. The study employed lag sequential analysis to compare the behavioral sequence patterns between the two groups and measured their multidimensional cognitive load. The results indicate that the high-quality group exhibited a significant evaluation-revision bidirectional cycle and a revision self-loop, with a clear progressive sequence of “planning → decision-making → generation → evaluation → revision → re-evaluation” in their behavioral flow. In contrast, the low-quality group was mired in ineffective cycles, with fragmented behavioral logic. Key findings showed large effect sizes for the evaluation-revision cycle ( r = 0.606) and for mental demand ( r = 0.647). Regarding cognitive load, the high-quality group reported no greater subjective effort than the low-quality group (though this null finding should be interpreted with caution given the study’s power limitations). A second round of within-sample replication confirmed that these core findings were consistent across a second task. Based on the human-AI collaborative behavioral patterns and cognitive load of the high-quality and low-quality groups, the study constructed a model of the human-AI collaboration patterns in generative AI-enabled instructional design for pre-service teachers. Specifically, higher-quality outputs were associated with a pattern oriented toward cognitive efficiency, characterised by deep processing (evaluation-revision iteration) and by the avoidance of ineffective cycles. Conversely, lower-quality outputs co-occurred with ineffective cycles arising in the context of interaction obstacles, in which repeated clarifications and interrupted revisions were accompanied by higher cognitive and emotional load, describing a pattern of high investment with low output. Because participants were grouped on the basis of their design outcomes, these findings are correlational and do not establish the direction of the relationships; they nonetheless provide empirical evidence to inform the optimisation of human-AI collaboration in GenAI-supported instructional design.

title: Same construct, same conclusion? A construct-observability perspective on self-report and non-self-report indicators in AI education research: a two-phase systematic review
abstract: Abstract AI-enhanced education research frequently combines self-report with tests, ratings, traces, or other non-self-report (NSR) indicators, but the two methods need not yield the same reported outcome conclusion. We conducted a two-phase systematic review. Phase 1 coded measurement methods and constructs in 2,099 title/abstract records. Phase 2 used a purposive, construct-stratified full-text sample and retained 51 same-construct entries from 47 reports, including inferential, descriptive, and qualitative evidence. A mixed-evidence descriptive synthesis classified 30 entries as concordant, 11 as discordant, and 10 as mixed across dimensions, conditions, or time points. The full-sample LOW-versus-HIGH comparison was not significant ( p = 0.555); a restricted sensitivity analysis of 10 entries from 10 reports with sufficiently aligned paired inferential evidence was likewise non-significant ( p = 0.524; nine classified entries tested). The descriptive LOW-HIGH ordering reversed between analyses, precluding a stable directional claim. Common-context within-study patterns suggested that output externality, feedback immediacy, and criterion explicitness may help explain heterogeneity, but they do not establish a causal mechanism or universal hierarchy. We develop construct observability as a testable, hypothesis-generating framework for organising cross-method heterogeneity. The practical implication is conditional: measurement should follow the claim. Self-report can be appropriate for perceptions, confidence, experiences, and self-observed behaviours; claims about demonstrated competence benefit from directly aligned performance-related evidence, while such NSR indicators also require their own validity justification.

title: ChatGPT’s feedback credibility and students’ perceived learning: the role of agent-related social perceptions
abstract: Abstract This paper examines whether students’ agent-related social perceptions of ChatGPT are associated with the perceived credibility of its feedback in academic tasks and whether such credibility, in turn, is related to students’ perceived learning. It also investigates whether the relationship between feedback credibility and perceived learning varies according to students’ sensitivity to the quality of their academic work and their sensitivity to grade-based rewards. To address this, we develop a theoretical model grounded in social perception theory and prior research on students’ experiences with AI-based tools. The model is tested using Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) on data collected from 230 students who completed an academic writing task. The findings reveal that students’ agent-related social perceptions—particularly perceived competence and human-like empathy—are positively connected to the credibility students attribute to its feedback. In turn, perceived feedback credibility is interestingly related to students’ perceived learning in the context of academic writing. Furthermore, the positive link between credibility and perceived learning is weaker among students with higher grade-based reward sensitivity. This research contributes to the educational technology literature by advancing understanding of how students evaluate the credibility of ChatGPT-generated feedback and how such evaluations are associated with learning perceptions. It also shows that agent-related social perceptions play a significant role in students’ credibility judgements. Finally, the findings offer practical implications for educators and students seeking to integrate ChatGPT effectively into academic activities.

title: Mapping generative AI in higher education teaching and learning: a scoping review
abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has rapidly entered higher education, but empirical research on its roles in teaching and learning remains fragmented across instructional activities, outcomes, assessment approaches, and stakeholder perspectives. This scoping review followed PRISMA-ScR guidelines to map 394 empirical studies of GenAI use in higher education published from November 2022 through December 2025. The review examined how GenAI tools were integrated into authentic teaching and learning activities, what outcomes or skills were targeted, how studies assessed those outcomes, and how students and instructors perceived GenAI use. Across the reviewed studies, GenAI was most often used to support existing academic tasks, especially feedback, tutoring, and writing. The most frequently targeted outcomes included engagement, usability and acceptance, critical thinking, disciplinary knowledge, academic performance, writing quality, and AI literacy. Self-regulated learning, ethics, creativity, feedback quality, and equity received less attention. Assessment practices relied mainly on surveys, tests or rubrics, artifact analysis, and interviews, suggesting that much of the evidence base is shaped by short-term and readily implemented methods. Student and instructor perceptions were predominantly mixed, reflecting perceived benefits alongside concerns about pedagogy, integrity, workload, and governance. The review highlights the need for stronger alignment between learning constructs and assessment methods, more process-sensitive evidence, clearer reporting of governance practices, and greater attention to equity in GenAI-supported higher education.

title: Higher education assessments in the age of GenAI: a systematic review
abstract: Abstract Assessment in higher education has long centered on core principles such as validity, authenticity, and alignment with learning outcomes, alongside ongoing debates about how best to support academic integrity and meaningful feedback. The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is now placing renewed pressure on these established principles, prompting institutions to reconsider how assessment is designed, delivered, and evaluated. While a growing body of research has examined GenAI’s role in teaching and learning broadly, less synthesis exists on how it is reshaping assessment specifically, and how these shifts relate to long-standing assessment theory and practice. This systematic review provides an up-to-date examination of empirical research published between 2024 and 2026 on how GenAI is influencing assessment practices and supporting educators in assessing student learning. Using PRISMA, 72 studies were identified and analyzed. The findings show that research was conducted across 24 countries and 20 academic disciplines. Two overarching research purposes emerged: (1) investigating the use of GenAI in assessment and (2) examining perceptions of GenAI in assessment. Qualitative approaches were the most common research methodology. Three major assessment design approaches emerged in response to GenAI: (1) process orientation, (2) authenticity, and (3) oral and dialogical approaches. Five ways educators used GenAI across the assessment process were identified: (1) creating assessments, (2) practice for assessments, (3) grading, (4) transparency of learning, and (5) feedback. Together, these findings situate GenAI’s influence with the broader trajectory of assessment scholarship and provides researchers, educators, institutional leaders, and policymakers a clearer picture of how assessment practices are being negotiated in response to GenAI

title: Effects of question-chain prompting on self-regulated learning, metacognition, and achievement in a generative AI environment
abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers learners immediate and personalized support, yet unguided interaction may encourage passive use and weaken self-regulated learning (SRL). This study examined whether question-chain prompting can support SRL in human-AI interaction. A quasi-experiment was conducted with 83 undergraduates enrolled in a television program production course. A control group used free-form questioning, whereas two experimental groups used either a progressive or a divergent question-chain strategy. Data included GenAI interaction logs, post-task reflections, metacognitive awareness measures, and course grades. This study found that both question-chain groups demonstrated significantly more learning-strategy and learning-monitoring behaviors than the control group. Reflection data further indicated differences in students’ approaches to human-AI collaboration, although these differences should be interpreted cautiously because the reflection prompts differed by condition. Moreover, both experimental groups scored significantly higher than the control group on knowledge of cognition, regulation of cognition, and academic achievement. No significant differences were found between the progressive and divergent question-chain approaches. The findings suggest that question-chain prompting, implemented as an instructional package of specific, sequenced, and required questions, can promote more active engagement during human-AI interaction and support metacognitive development and learning performance. Question chains offer a practical approach for guiding students’ use of GenAI in educational settings.

title: Who benefits from LLMs? Prompt engineering competence and equity in higher education
abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly becoming embedded in higher education, yet their benefits may be unevenly distributed. This study conceptualizes prompt engineering competence (PEC) as an equity-relevant interaction competence and examines whether differences in PEC are associated with perceived academic gains and perceived educational inequity. We adopt a two-stage quantitative design combining a cross-sectional survey with a within-subject prompt-quality experiment. Stage 1 reports a survey of Chinese undergraduates who have used LLMs ( N = 380), measuring PEC, perceived academic performance gains, perceived educational inequity, family digital capital, gaming experience, and a planning/independent-work tendency. Regression and mediation analyses show that PEC was strongly associated with perceived academic gains, while its association with perceived inequity was statistically significant but small. Background resources and learning-related experiences and dispositions explained substantial variance in PEC, especially gaming experience and planning/independent-work tendency, and the association between family digital capital and perceived academic gains was largely indirect through PEC. Stage 2 conducts a within-subject prompt-quality experiment across four higher-education task types and four popular models, comparing basic prompts with a student-oriented five-component refined prompt framework (Role–Goal–Input–Process–Output). Analysis of 400 matched prompt comparisons, comprising 800 model outputs, indicates that the refined prompt scaffold consistently outperforms basic prompts. Overall, the findings identify PEC as a potential competence pathway through which students may differ in their ability to convert LLM access into learning-related benefits, while structured prompt scaffolds may provide a scalable approach to reducing prompt-quality barriers in LLM-supported higher education.

title: GenAI-enabled educational game development: the effects of a scripted mystery role-playing game on students’ learning experience and learning outcomes in legal education
abstract: Abstract Although previous studies have shown that GenAI can support learning engagement and motivation, it remains unclear how GenAI-assisted development of offline educational games based on Scripted Mystery Role-Playing Games (SMRPG) influences students’ learning experiences and outcomes. Based on the SMRPG format, this study developed an offline educational game with the assistance of Gemini 3 Pro to explore its potential value for students’ learning outcomes and experiences in higher education contexts. A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design was employed with 84 undergraduate students majoring in law as participants. First, a randomized controlled experiment compared learning outcomes between an experimental group ( N = 42) and a control group ( N = 42). Subsequently, qualitative interviews were conducted with 24 students who participated in the game to examine their learning experiences during the gameplay process. Quantitative results showed that, after controlling for pre-test scores, the experimental group achieved significantly higher post-test scores than the control group (F(1, 81) = 105.61, p <.001, partial η² = 0.566). Qualitative findings indicate that participants described an immersive learning experience involving reasoning scenarios and role interaction in the GenAI-assisted game. This experience was associated with greater willingness to engage in learning, provided opportunities for the mobilization and application of relevant knowledge, and supported sustained motivation and reflective learning. This study provides empirical evidence on the learning experiences and learning outcomes associated with applying GenAI to develop legal educational games based on SMRPG, offering insights for future research and practice on GenAI-enabled educational game development.

title: Mind the AI policy gap: a policy analysis across global funding bodies
abstract: Abstract Research funding bodies have significant influence on what research is prioritised, how it is conducted, and what standards are enforced. While a number of global frameworks provide normative guidance on AI ethics, there is a clear gap in understanding how these principles are implemented at the funding-body level. This study aims to examine the current AI policies and guidelines of research funding bodies across different geographical regions. Inductive thematic analysis was adopted to analyse 56 AI-related policies from 46 funding agencies across the US, the UK, Europe, Australia, Singapore, Mainland China, and Hong Kong. The analysis revealed five common themes: human-centredness, safeguarding, embeddedness, governance, and AI readiness. It was also found that current funding-specific policies lack explicit guidelines on how broad principles and macro-level regulations can be interpreted and applied in AI-enabled research funding processes. The findings underscore the important role of funding agencies as key actors in defining responsible AI use in research processes. Finally, the practical implications of this study for regulators, funding bodies, and researchers are discussed, highlighting the value of policy document analysis in shaping ethical, transparent, and responsible AI frameworks.
